Nostril
nŏs´trĭl
n. (the opening of the nose; rendering Hebrew aph, nechiyr)
From Anglo-Saxon nosthyrl, literally nose-thirl, a nose-hole. The Hebrew aph means both nostril and anger, since the flaring nose was the face of wrath.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Nostril is where Scripture locates the gift and the fragility of life. Man is not made a living soul by his form but by a breath: “the LORD God formed man of the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul” (Gen 2:7). The flood reverses it exactly — “All in whose nostrils was the breath of life… died” (Gen 7:22). Job, in the middle of his misery, still reckons his life a loan held there: “All the while my breath is in me, and the spirit of God is in my nostrils” (Job 27:3). The same word carries the anthropomorphic language of divine wrath — “with the blast of thy nostrils the waters were gathered together” (Exo 15:8) — where the sea itself is parted by what Scripture pictures as God's breath. Nothing in man is more ordinary than breathing, and Scripture makes it the thinnest possible margin between dust and a living soul.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines the nostril as an aperture of the nose, the passage through which air is inspired and expired — noting that in Scripture the breath of the nostrils denotes life itself.

expand to see more

NOS´TRIL, n. An aperture or opening in the nose; a passage through which air is inspired and expired.

The nostrils are the organs of smelling, and the passages of respiration.

The LORD God breathed into his nostrils the breath of life. Gen. ii.

Key Scripture

Gen 2:7 — "And the LORD God formed man of the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul."

Job 27:3 — "All the while my breath is in me, and the spirit of God is in my nostrils;"

Exo 15:8 — "And with the blast of thy nostrils the waters were gathered together, the floods stood upright as an heap, and the depths were congealed in the heart of the sea."

Gen 7:22 — "All in whose nostrils was the breath of life, of all that was in the dry land, died."

Modern Corruption

Man reduced to his chemistry, so that life is an emergent property rather than a breath given — and, correspondingly, treated as disposable at both ends when its usefulness is doubted.

expand to see more

Genesis 2:7 sets two claims against every materialist account of man. First, the body is genuinely dust — Scripture concedes the chemistry entirely and is never embarrassed by it. Second, the dust does not become a living soul by any arrangement of itself, but by a breath from outside. Remove the second claim and man is a mechanism, and the value of any particular mechanism becomes a matter of function. That is not a slippery slope but a syllogism, and it is worked out at the beginning and the end of every human life.

Job 27:3 gives the pastoral form of the doctrine. In the worst affliction recorded in Scripture, Job does not claim ownership of his life; he says the spirit of God is in his nostrils — borrowed, sustained, and not his to end. A believer who has grasped that his next breath is a loan will hold both his own life and his neighbour's as something belonging to Another, which is finally the only stable ground for the sixth commandment.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew aph (H639), nostril, nose, and by extension anger — the flaring nostril as the face of wrath; neshamah (H5397), the breath of life God breathed into them.

expand to see more

Hebrew aph (H639) — nostril, nose, face, anger; the same word gives slow to anger, literally long of nostril (Exo 34:6).

Hebrew neshamah (H5397) — breath, spirit; what God breathed into the nostrils, distinguishing man from the beasts formed of the same dust (Gen 2:7).

Hebrew ruach (H7307) — spirit, wind, breath; the spirit of God in Job's nostrils (Job 27:3), sustaining a life he does not own.

Usage

"“Breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul” — dust plus a breath."

"“The spirit of God is in my nostrils” — Job holds his life as a loan."

"“With the blast of thy nostrils the waters were gathered together” — the sea parted by breath."
